utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we come to the next witness, I have a question to ask Mr. Krsnik. Yesterday afternoon, you said you would give me your initial response to documents intended by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, that is indeed so. Thank you for allowing me to speak. We do object to the document, but the Defence also objects to the manner of introduction of the documents. Your Honour, we searched for these documents for the whole afternoon yesterday and evening, because, you know, these 17 binders, I really cannot keep them here. And your decision was regardless of what binder a document was in, if one intended to tender a document, that it should be shown. Their Document 704, page 10, which was introduced and contained the name of Mr. Soldo, we did not know what the document was about and we couldn't know it until we found it, so it made the whole situation for us more difficult. And please could you see that your decision be complied with, both on our part and on the part of the Prosecution, that is, that both sides be told in advance. There is another bunch of documents, the ones that were introduced by Mr. Van Hecke, because this was a small bundle so we could carry it with us. So yesterday I could not say anything, and we finally found the document. We object to it. This is a document from the tobacco station. I apologise to my learned friends. I believe that that is it. This is one of the documents that is snatched from the tobacco station. We objected to those documents before, and we object to them today. As for the two passes, the two laissez-passer, that is, 198.1 and Exhibit 262.1, we have no objections to the admission of those documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. But I think yesterday the Prosecutor was only tendering the two documents, that is, P198.1 and Document P262.1. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's true. It was only those two documents with the witness yesterday afternoon. I might respond, two brief points, Your Honour. Admittedly, I think we are all still a bit finding our way on the best way to handle the volume of exhibits. I think it's evident at this point - I hope - that the Prosecution has made a tremendous effort to organise these materials in a way that makes the most sense substantively, that is, ultimately putting them in a chronological sequence. So if you will, the story is told if one reads the documents from beginning to end. They are in chronological order, except for some updated material at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. It is a huge effort. We're not asking anyone to pat us on the back, but we're simply saying a huge effort has been made. We don't necessarily intend to provide every single additional copy to the Defence every day, I don't think, because frankly at that point we're now creating still additional sets of documents. It was a huge effort and expense, et cetera, et cetera, to create multiple 17-binder sets. And the reason we did that - and I'm not sure any other Prosecution trial team has done that, perhaps they have - was to simplify and make the case more efficient and to make sure that everyone had the materials in an organised way. Now, it may not work perfectly still, but I can just tell the Chamber that we're trying, we're making every effort to be as helpful as we can. Your Honour, I just want to mention in passing, the issue has been raised now several times about a challenge to the seized documents. I don't want to obviously get into an argument about that now, I don't intend to, but I would simply note to the Chamber that throughout the Pre-Trial procedure, throughout the Pre-Trial in this case, which has gone on for some time, there was never a challenge -- there was no motion to suppress, there was never a challenge, a motion filed to that search and seizure operation, which frankly could have been done a substantial time ago. Those are our comments, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we are not going into a debate, you know, on those documents at this moment. If you have something to say, just put it in very concise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, very concisely. We objected to the manner of introduction of documents because we received copies of two documents before the hearing, so we could have been given a copy of the third document that was shown the witness yesterday, but we didn't know what that document was about. And I think that my objection is well grounded. I say nothing else. As for the rest of my -- as for other documents that my learned friend is speaking about, we simply had no idea where those documents came from, and what were they. Whether my learned friend wanted to produce them and turn them into evidence at that stage of the indictment, we simply did not know. And we had no idea where the documents came from. So I think it is not the right time to discuss the matters that were considered -- that were the subject of our Pre-Trial sessions. So I do not think we should discuss it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we are more concentrated on the two documents which we admitted into the evidence, that is Document P198.1 and the P262.1. The Defence counsels have no objections to these two documents. They are admitted into the evidence under the seal. The Registrar will be instructed to give a proper number at a later stage. Thank you. Mr. Scott, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. He will be seeking protective measures. Perhaps we should go to private session for a moment. Well, it's probably not necessary to do that. I suppose I can just tell you -- I don't think there will be an objection based on past practice -- this witness seeks to have a pseudonym, which I believe, if I am correct, would be Witness S, and to have his facial image distorted. Those are protections. We do have a sheet on the A4 format prepared, as the Court has instructed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there is no objections from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we said yesterday, no objections. There are no objections with regard to witnesses coming from the former Yugoslavia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just nodded; but for the record, I am repeating. We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. The protective measures is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I propose we will bring the witness in. Your Honours, perhaps I can use the time profitably to say that this witness will talk about the parts of the indictment, the background, paragraphs 7, 9, and 11; superior authority, paragraphs 14 to 17; the general allegations, paragraphs 18 to 21; count 1, paragraph 30, 32 through 34; counts 2 to 8, paragraphs 35 to 38, paragraphs 41, 42, and 44; count 21, paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, I am referring to you in that way because the Chamber has granted protective measures by which your true name will not be used. You will also have your facial image distorted for purposes of broadcast and for the record. You will be referred to, instead of your real name, as "Witness S." So the usher is going to show you now a piece of paper that has your name on it so there is a record of your true identity. Could you please look at that and simply say yes or no, is that your name, without saying your name, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that will be marked whatever the next W --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be PW19. Entered as PW19.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, you were born in Mostar in 1973 and you lived there more or less continuously until September of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness, could you please move forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Witness S, that you grew up and lived on the west side of Mostar, and that the area where you lived was primarily or mostly Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you, yourself -- I don't know which term you may prefer -- but you consider yourself either Muslim or Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a preference whether one refers to your nationality or origin as Bosniak or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness S, have you ever known a person named Vinko Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber, please, how you know him, starting with how you became first acquainted with him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I've known him since my early childhood because I lived in the same part of the town as Stela did. And I know him best because Stela was a taxi driver with a stop next to the mosque in Balinovac, and that is the area where I spent most of the time as a child and an adolescent. And that is how I came to know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you engage in any sort of business dealings, if you will, with Stela as a young person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, yes. On a couple of occasions, I borrowed some money from Stela. Because Stela was a taxi driver, he was wise up to certain things that went on in Mostar. I guess he knew lots of people. And I asked -- I asked him to lend me some money so that I could buy some cigarettes, smuggle them over, and then sell them at a slightly higher price, return the money to Stela, and of course keep the rest of the proceeds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Stela have any information for you as to where you could obtain cigarettes at a cheaper price?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention a bit forward to April 1992, did you become involved in any way in the defence of Mostar against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. From March '92, in the 30 days, I did not serve the army, so it was all perfect, it was all a big novelty to me, and I was in luck. There was Vinko Martinovic, Stela, Vinko Martinovic, Vina, and a couple of other guys who were older than I, and another man called Zela, that is Marko Zelic, and as a matter of fact they told us how to use weapons. That was the first time in our lives that we saw rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: And that was my first contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to some of those additional persons in a few moments. Who did you consider during this time is your commander, either officially or unofficially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, in the very beginning, I simply did not see anyone as a commander, because truth to tell, I had no military experience, as I had never served in any army. And those who were my seniors, well, I simply followed their example, because we simply thought that they knew things, that they'd help us survive the war and defend the town against the Serbs. The most prominent persons in my -- the most prominent figures in my eyes were Stela and Vina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll tell Your Honours, we'll come back to Vina in a moment. I'm not leave that hanging but will get there in just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we go forward, Witness S, can you tell us anything else you observed about Stela's conduct or behaviour during the approximate 1992 time period, in terms of property or things that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Right. In the beginning, those things seemed to me quite normal, because there was no authority and everybody could do as he pleased. So Stela and Zela and Vina and all the others would turn up in a new car every day. In the beginning, it looked funny and then strange to me. It looked odd. I didn't know how to explain it, because it went in day and day out. And once I was present when those cars were painted camouflage colours. I participated in the painting of a car myself, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any understanding of where these cars came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I knew they were some private cars, that is, cars that had been seized from private persons. And the car that I painted, that was a Renault 4 Special. I knew it had been taken from a company called Parkovi and Naselja. That is, that was a company that was responsible -- it was a public utility company responsible for cleaning the streets, maintaining parks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber around this time whether there was other taking of property or what some might call "looting" going on? I'm not asking you to tell us who at the moment, just were those things happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek. I saw Mr. Meek standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber, I must object on the ground that, Number 1, the Prosecutor is beginning to ask leading questions of this witness and, Number 2, I do not believe that the events which this witness is presently testifying about concern our indictment, which is from April 1993 to January 1994. And this would appear to be some evidence of bad acts or prior crimes to prove the -- the Prosecutor to prove that if something was improper earlier, that something must have been improper later. And on these grounds, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the first objection, Mr. Scott, I think your question is some sort of leading one, because you said whether there was other taking of properties, what some might call "looting" going on, which you gave the indication to this witness the answer. As for the second objection, maybe you could clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could respond to both. Your Honour, I submit that the first objection is not proper. It's not leading, other than to direct the witness to a particular topic. I can't very well, frankly, ask him simply, "What happened next," "What happened next," because that won't take us very far. I didn't suggest what was happening or who was doing it. I simply asked him during this time period whether a certain type of activity was taking place. I will try it again. I'm not sure I can do any better than that. As to the second objection, Your Honour, these are relevant, clearly. It's the Prosecution's position that Stela was a prominent figure in Mostar, both before, during and after the war; that he had a network of people that were involved -- excuse me, I'll slow down. He had a network of people, common associates that he associated with before, during, and after the war; that he was a leading figure and engaged in looting, again what we contend, the Prosecution contends, if you want to call it "looting" or "theft", again both before the war, during the war and after the war. It goes to a consistent course of conduct involving this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could I just say something. Mr. Scott, I think you went into the specifics of this witness's evidence without really properly laying the background. We're not supposed to know the story in advance. I don't know about what happened in the town of Mostar that led this young man to leave whatever work he was doing, whether it was smuggling cigarettes or otherwise, and Mr. Martinovic from driving a taxi suddenly to having arms. You haven't actually told us or asked this witness to tell us what happened that they needed to be introduced to the use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy to go back to it. It is true that in the interests of making some of these witnesses as short as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible, we are trying to build upon the record in the case. But I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: But his evidence would make more sense if we had had a little bit of that background from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to try to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, let's go back. You've heard, I hope through interpretation, the Chamber's various comments, and my apologies for not taking you through other parts of your story. Directing your attention, let's go back to your involvement with cigarettes. Can you just tell us or give us an idea, by the way, of approximately how long did you engage in that activity and how often did you interact with Mr. Martinovic on that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, it happened several times. I cannot say whether it happened five, six, or maybe even as many as ten times. And I communicated with Stela with regard to these matters two or three times -- once, perhaps twice, perhaps three times. It was a long time ago. I cannot be accurate. And I simply -- I don't know. That was the way to get by -- some dough and take a girl out. At that time, that was the only way in which I could make some money. I mean smuggling was the only way out that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please respond, if you can, to Judge Clark's questions about how did you -- what were the circumstances - excuse me - in Mostar during approximately the first half of 1992 that caused you to become involved in any sort of military or quasi-military way with Mr. Martinovic, Stela, and others that you named a few minutes ago? If you can just tell us a bit more about that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: First I'd say that I really don't know about this "military" and "paramilitary" because I cannot tell one from the other. I could not really tell you what the difference is. Secondly, I would say that in those early days of the war, I simply followed the example of those who were older than I was, like Stela, like Vina, like Bosnjic and many others. They were my models. And I realised that Serbs would tear our city apart, and I was afraid, of course. I thought it was my duty not only to defend myself but also my family and my brother, my friends and my city. And now whatever you call it, a military or a paramilitary formation, but when the Serbs started shelling the city, the only ones who were there to keep us together and to help us was Stela, and they were really the only ones. And I think that was really quite decent on their part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at this time -- continuing on the questions raised by Judge Clark -- do you know whether Stela was identified with any particular military or paramilitary unit or organisation at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: At that point, I didn't know about Stela, didn't know where the commands were coming from, why all these things were happening that were happening, and I didn't care at that point. I just wanted to save my life, and I was about 20 years old. All I was thinking about was how to survive. When I survived the first shelling, I just prayed to God that I live to see another day. That was at first. After a period of time, I saw that Stela was with HOS, together with Vino Martinovic, Semir Bosnjic, but that only happened later. At first, I did not know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, if we could perhaps, with that additional background, move forward just a bit. Did you at some point as time went by, based on what you've just told us in the last few minutes, become more officially, if I can use that term, associated with a particular military formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, yes. When -- over time, when the defence of the city became organised, and it looked better every day, I remember this 4th Battalion, which later was renamed the Tihomir Misic battalion, and I stayed with them for the most part of the war, almost until the end of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we jump forward just for a moment just to give some parameters on the time period you're going to testify about today. Did you leave the military, in fact, leave Mostar, sometime before the war was over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I left Mostar. I think that was exactly to a day eight years ago. I think it's actually today's date. I may be off by a day. In other words, on the 19th of September, 1993. And the entire period up to that date, I was with the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And that was my next question. So once -- just to be clear -- once you joined the 4th Battalion, you continuously were a member of that unit until you left Mostar on about the latter part of September 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I can tell you something else that I thought at that time that I was not a soldier. In 8th of May, 1993, I was disarmed in a coffee bar in Mostar; and for 10 days thereafter, I did not consider myself a member of any unit. But for the rest of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just so the record is very clear on this, when you've mentioned being part of the 4th Battalion, or the Tihomir Misic Battalion, again, what military side or army was that a unit of, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It was part of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, during this time, were there times when you fought under Stela's command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, there were several situations. At the very beginning of the war, I saw Stela as a commander, and there were additional situations where Stela would issue orders during the war. But he was not my commander. And to be honest, I could not and did not want to ever oppose Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we'll come to that in a few minutes, please. Can you tell the Chamber who your commanders were in the 4th Battalion, and give us the names, as best you can. And it may help the record and translation if you can spell the names for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Shall I tell you who they were from the very beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how many you have in mind. Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: The first one was the late Tihomir Misic, who was later killed, and the unit was then named after him. For a while, his father was the commander, Mladen Misic. Then a man whose name I cannot recall today. But while Tihomir Misic was in command, he was the communications man, which means at the very beginning of the defence of the city. Then there was a man nicknamed "Fritz." I don't know his real name. That is what I can recall. And my superiors were Vinko Martinovic, as commander of my company. He was a company commander. And a man nicknamed Gaga [Realtime transcript read in error "Gava"], Dragan Petkovic, who was my platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. The transcript says "Gava." If you can assist us, please, I think it is Gaga, G-a-g-a. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. G-a-g-a.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was, if you will, your most direct commanding officer in terms of at the platoon level?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, could you ask this witness to clarify. That's the second use of the name "Vinko Martinovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, that's my next inquiry, Your Honour. Sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, before we turn to Judge Clark's question, can you just confirm, my last question to you was your most direct commanding officer in terms of a platoon level was this Mr. Gaga. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I apologise really, but I have both of them in my head, Vina and Stela, and I distinguish them. But this was Vinko Martinovic, Vina, not Vinko Martinovic, Stela. And my immediate superior was Dragan; he was my platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness S, very specifically, because I think it will be obvious to people in the courtroom, this is an important point. You knew another person during the same time, in roughly the same location, also named Vinko Martinovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, the only difference was that they had two different nicknames. One was nicknamed Stela, and the other one Vina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, so the record is abundantly clear, when you said a moment ago that one of the Vinko Martinovics was your commander at some level, that was the Vinko Martinovic also known as Vina, V-I-N-A. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to tell us, please, so there's -- if you can tell us a bit more about these two men who have the same name. Were these two men similar in appearance and similar in their conduct, or can you please just tell these things -- explain these things to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. They looked completely different, and they behaved in a completely different manner. I know that they perhaps were of the same generation. Even Vina, Vinko Martinovic, Vina, actually was a taxi driver, just as Stela was, and they were using the same taxi stop. But I distinguished them by other features.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said just now that they physically looked very different. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom today, please, if you can, with the way you are screened, but if you can please look around the courtroom and tell us if you see the person you knew then as Vinko Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look around physically and identify him for the record. You'll have to say -- describe his clothing and where he is located in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: He is sitting in a back row to my left. From what I can see, second from the left. If I can see correctly, he is wearing a suit, he has receding hair, and he is stocky.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the record please reflect that the witness has identified the accused Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also said a moment ago that their conduct was quite different. Can you tell us more what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a bit difficult for me to explain it right now. I know both of them. I've known them since I was small. And the difference between them is not enormous, but they behaved differently during the war. That was a significant difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell us about that, please. How did they behave significantly different during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Vina was much more withdrawn, much more calm and was a better person, according to me. And through my conversations with Vina, he said that he knew that the war was going to come to an end. And he said that we had to keep up a reputation, because the war will end one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this witness is no longer testifying to the facts in the case of the Prosecutor; but rather, he is testifying about character of this person, and that is not his -- this is not what he was called to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that it's very important for us to have a clear picture of what your witness is -- and distinguish him from another person who bear the same name as this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, I think the Chamber has indicated, please proceed with your answer. And focus, if you can, if you can tell us, conduct, what you saw with your own eyes or heard with your own ears about the conduct, statements or behaviour of the two men that you have been telling us about, how they were different concerning the war, as you just took us to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to point to the particular period of the war. If you're referring to the period of the conflict between the HVO and the AbiH, that's a totally different situation than the war against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Let me try to assist. Let me direct your attention to approximately the middle of 1993, if that will assist you, approximately the period May to September before you left, 1993. Hold on one moment, please. Witness S, just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Judge Clark has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I normally reserve my questions to the end, but I just want to get this picture clear. As you can appreciate, two of us are new Judges here. I'd like you to let this witness continue with the evidence that he was giving on his description of the man with the nickname "Vina." And I believe that he was dealing with what he calls the early part of the war, which would have been the conflict with the Serbs. If we deal with that first, then everything slots into place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, you've heard the Judge's comments. Let me take you back earlier, contrary to my first instruction, to the summer of '93. Let's go back initially to the time in approximately the spring of 1992, about which you were testifying a few minutes ago. During that time, can you describe the differences or the conduct of these two men? For purposes now, Stela and Vina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, both Stela and Vina were with HOS, Croatian armed forces, which some considered military, some a paramilitary unit, and some thought that they assumed it was there just to exploit the situation for its own benefit. My opinion is, and this is my personal view, that Vina was a much more withdrawn and calm person who was more approachable. It was easier to talk to him. He did not try to distinguish himself by doing things that shouldn't have been done. And to my opinion, Stela was the exact opposite of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how was he the exact opposite of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning of the war, as far as I know the situation, Stela was the chief commander of the HOS. And from what I knew, Stela and Vina were good friends. They knew each other, they associated, and they were in the same business, so to speak, before the war. But Stela, in my view, was a bit more aggressive, perhaps more strict. Maybe that's the way I can put it. And Vina was my neighbour, and I knew not only him but his brothers, his mother and father, and perhaps that may have been the reason that Vina was closer to me. I cannot really say. But Vina was much more calm and much more tame and a person that one could talk to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go forward, then. Perhaps with that background, if we do move forward to the time from approximately May to September of 1993 during the conflict between the HVO and the Muslims or Bosniaks. Can you tell us, please, did you see differences in the conduct of Vina and Stela during that time and, if so, what were the differences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, the differences became much greater. I did not know what role Stela was to play in that war until 8 May 1993, when I was in a coffee bar in town owned by the Sadzak brothers. That evening, I learned what role Stela would play in all this, because I learned that from Milicevic, called "Baja" [Realtime transcript read in error "Bija"], and one of the Sadzak brothers. And Vina had a completely different role. In my view, Vina was to be a positive person in the next period, because he was looking at me as a person, not as a Muslim, as a balija, and tried to help as much as he could in these difficult times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, are you suggesting that there was somebody else who did look at you -- to state the opposite of what you just said, was there somebody who did look at you as a Muslim and, with my apology, a balija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in terms of your testimony in the last few minutes, are you telling us -- identifying one particular person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. Stela was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to suggest, if you'll allow me, that perhaps the best way to finish this particular topic is at the end of the testimony as opposed to now, in terms of these differences, because I think we're going to get into essentially the rest of the testimony. And then by that time, it may become clear, how they were different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may arrange your order of the questions by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness S, a moment ago you took us to -- you began to take us to an event on the 8th of May, 1993. I take you back there now, please. Tell us what happened that evening. Just take us through as much as you can. What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: We were in this coffee bar called "Oasis", my brother, myself and another guy. (redacted), and we had spent our youth together. Oasis at that time was a place Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. patronised by people who had done something, who had made a contribution to the city, to its defence. It wasn't an open type of place. So we were -- (redacted) and I were playing pool on the top floor. And one of the Sadzak brothers, one of the owners, was downstairs at the bar, listening to music, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, my apology. I just want to caution you before you inadvertently say it. You made references to your brother and you may refer to other people now, and do not use your brother's name or your name, of course. That may tend to identify you, and I just want to caution you about that. Please go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and Your Honours. I must lodge an objection at this point to this open-ended question. The witness is now rambling and there's no direction to this answer, and I don't believe that is proper. I think that it's proper that the Prosecutor ask specific questions which are not leading and there be answers, not just open-ended questions that the witness can give a monologue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid we have to see where the Prosecution is leading us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to do it either way. There has been discussion the last few days about leading, and I'm trying to have the witness give a narrative without my giving him any other direction as much as possible. But I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may continue with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, please just continue with your story, keeping in mind the caution I gave you a moment ago. You were at this restaurant with your brother and some friends, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was exactly, but it was towards the evening when Mario Milicevic, called "Baja", came to the Oasis, and one of the Sadzak brothers also, and one of the Sadzak brothers -- I was just ordering coffee from the other Sadzak brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can stop you there for a moment. I apologise for interrupting you, but for the record, it may assist. Is "Sadzak" spelled S-A-D-Z-A-K, with a diacritic on the "Z"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, just as it is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: And Baja also came upstairs and told Sadzak to come down, that he had something important to tell him, and he asked the three of us to stay upstairs because this was something that they needed to talk about in private and we can go on with our pool game. And we did that. We thought -- hadn't given it another thought. We played pool, we talked about all kinds of things. And 15, 20 minutes later, maybe even half an hour later, one of the Sadzak brothers came back and told us that he was sorry to have to tell us the way he's going to tell us, but that Mr. Tuta, whose name I heard that for the first time, had ordered that an attack on Vranica be launched and the other Muslim forces, and that this attack be launched the next morning at 5.05 a.m., and that the attack will start at Vranica because that was a strategic point for the AbiH. I felt bad to hear that this was considered a strategic point, where so many civilians lived, and it was no secret that the headquarters was there. Of course, there were armed soldiers there and they can offer resistance, but I still felt very bad because I knew what could happen, and I felt fear, like everybody else would. But Sadzak comforted me a little bit. He called Baja and told him that he had told us this, and Baja then told the three of us - we all had our own pistols with us - that he apologised but he would like us to hand over these pistols. The three of us just looked at each other. I think that the same thoughts must have crossed our mind. I know that for a moment I thought, "Well, I'm going to get a bullet now," because once you're disarmed in the war, when you cannot defend yourself except maybe throw a stone, you don't feel safe at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, I'm going to stop you there, if I may. You've mentioned a person named "Baja." Do you know his formal name or, if that's only part of his name, his complete name? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. I told you his full name before, Mario Milicevic, Baja, owner of a coffee shop or a restaurant - I really don't know what to call it – (redacted) (redacted), so that I know Mario Milicevic very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, is the correct spelling of the last name M-I-L-I-C, as in "ch", E-V-I-C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: M-I-R -- M-A-R-I-O, M-I-L-I-C-E-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. My mistake. Now, when he entered, when Baja also became part of the conversation - just taking you back to where we left off - was anything else said about this planned attack the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, many things were said then. I don't know whether I should go into detail. It was said that the mosques would be mined, and the mosques in Balinovac and Podhum were specifically mentioned. And that large numbers of Muslims would be expelled; that is, women and children would be expelled to the side under the BiH Army's control, that men would be collected at collection points. And it was said that whoever offered resistance would be simply shot, that they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the same conversation, apart from the name Tuta that you mentioned, was there any other name of a senior Croat figure that you recall being mentioned in this same conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. I gave you the sentence as he said it that day. I think I quoted it in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us, please, before moving forward, did this Baja have a military group under his command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: That evening, I learned that evening that he would be one of the commanders of an anti-terrorist group, which was later named Benko Penavic group. And that the commander of another anti-terrorist group from Mostar would be Stela. Well, naturally, started this conversation with Baja and Sadzak. If they could tell me all those things, then they could tell me everything, and they did not hide anything from me. I should also say that at that time, I had no idea who Tuta was. And I asked Sadzak and Baja, will you please tell me, who is that Tuta that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, may it please the Trial Chamber, Mr. President and Your Honours. I must object. Understanding that hearsay is admissible, this is the worst kind of hearsay we have of the fact that Mario Milicevic walks into this coffee bar, takes two other people upstairs, those two other people come downstairs. We have no foundation as to where Mario Milicevic heard this information that was passed on to two brothers. And this is the worst kind of hearsay. This is three or four or five times removed. And I must remind the Trial Chamber, if not object, and I do object to this type of hearsay because there is no foundation, and it is so far removed that it is unreliable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In the answers, there is still some problems that we are not quite clear. Maybe the Prosecutor could direct your witness to more specifics, so that to clear these things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, let's go back. You gave us a narrative account. If we can pick up a few more details, please. What did you understand, if you did, about where this information was coming from? Who came into the restaurant and, if you know, from where, and who was providing this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I realized that Baja had come from a meeting with the Tuta -- I mean, I know Baja. I don't know Tuta. And I have no idea who the man is, at that time. And Baja came. And after he said all that, that is, I learned about what was to happen, and Baja himself said that he had been to a meeting with Tuta, and this was repeated several times. I don't know why. But Baja looked rather nervous, rather jittery, and obviously he wasn't very happy about what he was telling us, but he obviously knew what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President -- please, go ahead. I'm sorry. Finish your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't really know how to explain it. At that point, I was really scared stiff. All those images that went through my head, what was going on at the moment, what was to happen, my father, mother, friends, relatives on both sides of the city. So a lot of things that I perhaps should have asked Baja, I didn't. And perhaps I'll never get the chance to ask him those things. But I think Baja, perhaps, said more than he should have, as it was more than clear what was to happen the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, if I can stop you there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, to respond to the Defence objection at this point, I think it is clear - I submit that it is clear - from the witness's testimony just now that we are talking, indeed, about hearsay. It appears to be a statement that, according to the witness, Tuta made to, among others, Baja, and then Baja relating to this witness. So there's no dispute that we're talking about, essentially, if you will, two steps, but I don't think more than that. And we do think it's proper, under the Tribunal's rather liberal views toward hearsay, and with the professional Judges on the Bench, that the Chamber should hear this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it will be the job of the Judges to evaluate the weight of those evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, a few minutes ago, you mentioned the Benko Penavic ATG, and you learned about this time that this was Baja's unit. Is that correct, just to bring us back to that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No problem, but let me correct you. It isn't an anti-terrorist brigade, it's an anti-terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apology if I misspoke. You mentioned a few moments ago now there was another ATG that was headed by another person in Mostar. And who was that, again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I will repeat it once again. The chief commander of the Benko Penavic anti-terrorist group was Mario Milicevic, Baja. And this other anti-terrorist group was commanded by Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with Stela's ATG, did you know any names associated with that unit, other than -- not Stela's personal name, but was it known by any other names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, around the town, they knew them first as Stelici, Little Stelas, calling it after its commander Stela. Also among others, it was known as ATG Mrmak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can go forward, please, that same evening, let me direct your attention to about 3.00 the next morning. Can you tell us if anything happened then; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I think that I should go back, go further back before that 3.00 in the morning. That is, that evening when I learned what was to happen the next morning, Baja also said then that -- he asked us to hand over our personal weapons, but Baja also offered to protect us, us and our families, and said that my brother and this pal of ours and I could, if we wanted, go to his place that night, that he would absolutely guarantee our safety, and that he would take care that none of the other units came to the street on which we lived. And I and my brother and this pal of ours, of course, accepted it, because we -- at that time, we saw it as the only way out, that is, to keep our heads on our shoulders. And then that morning, around 3.00, that is, when the attack started on the 9th of May, Zeljko Martinovic, called Zelja, came to his house. He is a relative of Vinko Martinovic, Vina. There was also another guy -- I can't say a guy, really. He was a middle-aged sort of man, Zubac, who was quite a prominent -- the most prominent man amongst us. He had a Mercedes; he had lots of money. And Stela was there in the street -- no, I have to say that I did not see Stela with my own eyes, but I was inside. I was in the room, and they were standing on the balcony right out of the room. They were all standing there. They kept going out and coming in and taking weapons that were in the flat, and there were all sorts of weapons. There were even some weapons that I had never seen before. And I recognised Stela because he has a specific manner of speech. I do not think there is another man on earth who speaks the same way, a specific voice. And there was also -- no, Zelja Martinovic was the one who told me that they would all come in their own cars, that they were about to leave soon because the action was about to begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, I'm going to stop you there for a moment, before you get too far. You have gone on for some time now, as I asked you to. Can you please go back. In the transcript, there is a reference to Bija, B-i-j-a. Can you tell us, all these events you've told us just now about just now, just to be clear, where were you again, and make sure we have the correct spelling. At whose house were you that you described -- where you're describing all these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: In Baja house. B-A-J-A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've told us, so it's clear, you don't recall, correct me if I am wrong, just so the record is clear, you don't recall seeing Stela, but you recognised his voice. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I said, and I can explain it to you. For the past eight years, it could be two a day since I left Mostar, through all this time, I have been seeing these pictures in my head, and I know exactly what happened, when it happened, how it happened. And I really did not -- could not wish such a thing -- such experience on anyone. But I did hear Stela; I did hear Stela's voice. There is no doubt about that. Perhaps I wouldn't be able to tell what I had for lunch yesterday, but these things, I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness S, I'm going to try to move us a bit forward. We do need to move a little bit along because of time. Tell us -- take us further in the story where you are now. Take us further there. You see weapons being loaded into cars. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, they all left. I really do not know where they went. Only Baja's father stayed with us. He had the same nickname. Funny, that. He was there to keep us, I don't know, to keep us company, to give us some comfort or what. And then at 5 minutes past 5.00, gunfire started all over the place. It was not normal. I had been a soldier until then. I had spent 13 or 14 months as a soldier and being told the possible front lines facing the Serbs, but such an attack, such artillery, no, I don't think that even in a film they ever made anything like that. They were using all possible means of artillery. There were tanks and mortars and rocket launchers. I could recognise them. And there were all sorts of calibres. There were PAMs, the anti-aircraft machine-guns. There was one such over Baja's house where we were. And I don't know. I am really at a loss of words to describe that horror, that hell which started at 5 of 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, let me just take you on. You're back at Baja's house. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. A couple of hours may have gone by from that initial strike, and then the first one to return was Zeljko Martinovic, Zelja. And I was very much under the weather, because he was with a man whose name was Neven, and that was the first time in my life I had seen such a disgusting man. He was crying, weeping. He could not justify his actions. He started shouting first. He put his fist in the door frame. He took his rifle, started hitting it against a wall. I was really surprised because Zelja was a well-respected man in the city. He drove motorbikes. We thought he was a tough guy who could not be defeated by anything. And when I saw how he showed his rage, his sorrow. He talked about murders. He talked about abuses, about beatings, expulsions, roundings up of men of -- in the stadium. It's very hard for me to talk about all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this Zelja identify any particular persons who were engaged in the conduct that you described just now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment, please. He mentioned Stela. He mentioned some men from Livno. He mentioned Baja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, I'm sorry for the discomfort you're obviously feeling. Can you tell us, please, what was said about Stela, in particular, if you're able to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, Zelja said that he had known Stela since he was a little boy. And he couldn't believe that Stela could be so cruel, that Stela had metamorphosed to a beast and that he couldn't believe it, and I looked at him. I couldn't expect to hear something like that from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything specific about what he had seen Stela do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. He talked about a unit from Livno. I still don't know what its name is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I know what his name is, Ante Bruno Busic, and how they pulled out of a flat Nedzo Huskovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Mr. Seric standing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection. I'm objecting both to the question and to the answer of this witness, because this goes beyond the scope of the indictment. Namely, Nedzad Huskovic's murder is not one of the charges against my client, nor the events the witness is beginning to testify about, and it is not in those counts which our learned friend indicated to the Chamber as the counts that this witness would testify about. Nedzad Huskovic's murder is presently a case heard in a court in Mostar against completely different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to say maybe it's time for a break. And we notice that your witness is under emotional stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as for the questions and answers, we are not quite sure where you are going to direct us. Maybe you could give us an explanation after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After the break, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to belabour this point too much, and we are anxious to finish this witness, but we submit that the evidence on this Nedzad Huskovic is indeed relevant and proper for the Chamber to hear, to receive. In the indictment, Mr. Martinovic is charged with a wide range of behaviour constituting, among other things, persecution. In paragraph 33, he is charged that both accused repeatedly tortured detainees, caused severe physical and mental suffering, was intentionally inflicted on Bosnian Muslims. It goes on in paragraph 34 that both of these accused, throughout this time period, planned, instigated, ordered, or committed a campaign of widespread or systematic persecutions of Bosnian Muslims. In paragraph 45, it says both accused and their subordinates tortured or wilfully caused great suffering to Bosnian Muslim civilians and prisoners of war, severe physical and mental suffering was intentionally inflicted. Paragraph 50 also we believe is relevant, and paragraph 54 we also believe is relevant. We also believe it is relevant to the accused's state of mind as to purposes and his motivation in carrying out various acts. We certainly don't intend to offer extensive evidence on this point. In fact, it will be just one or two questions and answers. But we believe the Chamber should receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies for taking a little bit more of your time, but I need to notify the Trial Chamber on the situation in which we find ourselves and anticipating the issues which have been foreshadowed by the Prosecutor. We had a first-hand witness regarding the incident which had been announced by the Prosecutor. There is a first-hand eyewitness who, before this Tribunal, gave evidence on the 27 July of this year, Witness F, who does not mention this incident, nor was he questioned about the fate of Nedzad Huskovic. And now the Prosecution is bringing this second-hand witness, even though during the deposition phase, we had an opportunity to hear from a first-hand witness about this incident. The Prosecution did not question Witness F on this incident, even though they had a statement of this witness of 15 January, 1996 pertaining to the persecution of the Huskovic family and the murder of Nedzad Huskovic. And I said, there are trial going on against completely different persons regarding this incident. It is now incomprehensible to ask that through this witness, where we had Witness F in the courtroom and members of the Huskovic families, who are also witnesses to this, it is incomprehensible to us that they are bringing this witness to testify, to give evidence about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a completely separate objection, of course. One, apparently, was beyond the scope, and now we are being told that it's not the appropriate witness. To be perfectly honest, I don't question counsel's representations on the testimony of a deposition witness except to say, off the top of our heads, Mr. Stringer and I don't recall that situation with Witness F. And Witness F, in fact, was Mr. Stringer's witness during the depositions. And we just don't recall that. But counsel may be perfectly right. In any event, we believe that it's proper for the Court to receive this evidence for as far as it goes. And again, it's going to be one or two questions, and we can hopefully finish this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from this witness, we heard a lot of hearsay evidence up to now. And sometimes it's very difficult for the Judges to know whether these questions are relevant or not at the very beginning. But we hope that the Prosecutor could bear in mind the objections from -- raised by Mr. Seric and direct us to the direct incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try. If we become bogged down in this, I'll tell the Chamber now, I will simply move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, please, before the break, you were telling us about this Zelja had come back to Baja's house where you still were and was very upset about some things that he had witnessed. Now, can you tell us just very briefly, and I do want you please to tell us specifically about this item now, do you recall being told about something that had happened to this man Nedzo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It was like this: You need to understand one thing. Nedzo was mentioned there, and it was mentioned how Nedzo was killed. A myriad of details were mentioned and I cannot keep them all in my head, but you also need to understand me that at that moment, when one is afraid for one's own life, I simply don't know who is saying what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of that, we'll pass on, unless the Court has questions -- unless the Chamber has questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just, if I go back a little bit, do you remember in the morning when you were about to ask this witness, quite early on, I think your question was, Please tell me who was Tuta. And then there was a Defence objection, and we went on. You never actually went back to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour, I can go back if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think your testimony was, and please correct me, that when these men came into the restaurant that evening, it was related to you that Tuta -- someone named Tuta had ordered certain things. And I believe you said this was the first time you had heard the name Tuta. Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I actually asked, Who is this Tuta? That's how I put it. And Baja then told me briefly that it was a person who came from abroad and, if I recall exactly, that he had come from South America. That is the first time that I encountered the name of Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it might assist Judge Clark, can you tell us anything more around that time? In the days immediately following the evening of 8 May 1993, did you hear anything more about Tuta or come to know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It turned out that Tuta was a man who, for the most part, led these two anti-terrorist groups that were considered elite units. And these two units, I'm sure of that, were under -- under -- they were not under any command from Mostar. In other words, no command out of Mostar came to those units. If you really want me to tell you how many times I've met Tuta and how I came to know how he looked, this was during a funeral of a young man named Zeljko Velc where I saw Tuta for the first time during that funeral. And a friend of mine told me, What is Tuta doing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, my apologies. You got a bit ahead of us, which is fine. But can you tell the Chamber, did you hear -- at this funeral, did you hear Tuta say anything to anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. I was standing right behind Tuta and Baja, who were standing next to each other, and I heard Tuta say to Baja, "What were you doing in that part of town? What am I going to tell Zagreb?" And Baja just shrugged. But by that time, they had a salvo for the -- in honour of the fallen soldier, Zeljko, who I knew from the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear any other part of the conversation between Tuta and Baja after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No, no. I left after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I left the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did you see Tuta personally - I don't mean necessarily on TV or something - did you ever see Tuta personally again after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. I'm not 100 per cent sure. Perhaps somewhere else, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness S, if we can go back now to the 9th of May, please. Can you tell us, later that day or in the days following the 9th of May, did you learn or could you see the status or condition, if you will, of any of the mosques in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was still at Baja's house around 10.00 when the Balinovac mosque was blown up. That was a huge explosion. I'm not an expert in it, but I don't know how much explosive was set -- was used there. But it was an enormous explosion, and you had pieces of stone flying around. I may have been about 200 metres in a straight line from the mosque at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment. This particular mosque, can you tell -- if you remember, can you tell us: Had that mosque been previously damaged or injured in some way during the time of the fighting with the Serbs or had that particular mosque been in reasonably good condition prior to the time that you say it was exploded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Until that morning, the mosque was perhaps damaged only by several bullets. Maybe a shell may have fallen nearby, but it was not any kind of damage that couldn't be repaired. But in fact this explosion destroyed the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in addition to that mosque, can you tell us again, did you see around that time any other mosques that were damaged or destroyed around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs had damaged several mosques. There were several mosques that had the top of minarets missing. But the same day when the Balinovac mosque was destroyed, there was another one destroyed which was in the neighbourhood called "Podhum," which is only a few hundred metres from the former -- from the line that was to be drawn there, and it was also blown up like the Balinovac mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness, I want to take you forward. Some days after these events, did you become engaged again in some military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I did not understand what it meant, to be active. But I was in fear. I did not know how to avoid all that. I just wanted to leave this town, but it was impossible. So I rejoined the 4th Battalion at that point, and I was assigned to the platoon whose commander was Gaga. They went by the name "Blue Boys." They had some blue arm bands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to ask you, because there may be some question, I imagine, in the courtroom: Why at this time, as a Bosniak or Muslim, after what you've just told us, did you engage yourself with an HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: There were several reasons. I need to be frank. The first and foremost for me was to get some kind of documents so that I can move about freely in town, so that I can protect my family, to find -- to figure out a way to get out of the whole situation. And perhaps you will not understand this fully, but I never have - and I don't now - hated anyone, Croats or Serbs. I have no reason for it, because I think that we were just instruments in the hands of some people who had the power to manipulate us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that begs the next question. Who do you think was manipulating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, we were manipulated by people, and this is -- somebody may take exception, but I think that people like Tuta played a part in this. I have to point this out, because I know Stela very well and I think that he, too, was manipulated. I don't know. I can't explain. I don't know what goes through someone's mind. I regret that things like this have happened and that many people -- and the way they did it. It all could have been resolved in another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness S, I think we're going to have to move on. I apologise to the Chamber, perhaps, but time is going by. I'm trying my best to move us forward. Now, let me ask you, Witness S, in the time that you then became again in the 4th Battalion, can you tell us where in Mostar -- after this time and until you left Mostar in the latter part of September, can you tell us where you were positioned in your military role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: My first and primary task was to be at the Bulevar in Dr. Aleksic's house, which was literally across the street from the Health Centre in Mostar. On several occasions, I was in other locations but only for assistance, but in the area under control of the 4th Battalion, the Tihomir Misic Battalion. But for the most part, it was in Dr. Aleksic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe the name, Your Honours, is spelled A-l-e-k-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It's Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, very well. You just mentioned a moment ago that this was across from -- I believe you said it was across from the Health Centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any understanding during this time whose -- what military unit, its leader, had that area under their responsibility, that part of the confrontation line which included the Health Centre? Who was responsible for that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, the Health Centre itself was covered by the ATG Mrmak and another one. Sometimes there was one; there were both. Then sometimes we were to go over there and be with them. It depended on the day. But those two units were the ones that were deployed at the Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness S, with the usher's assistance, I'm going to hand you a clean copy -- when I say "clean," no markings on it -- of Exhibit P11.18. If you could look at that and if it could be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the easiest way to deal with this, Mr. President, if everyone just has it on the ELMO rather than distributing multiple copies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like you to do, if you can, Witness -- if we could make that, please, as clear as possible. Can you show us, first of all, approximately where Dr. Aleksic's house was located; approximately where you were positioned during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: There is a little problem here. I can barely read what is -- the words on this, from this screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if you have another copy ahead you, right in front of you, it may be more clear than trying to read off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: This would be the Health Centre. Directly across was Dr. Aleksic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could be handed a marker, please. Would you mark -- first of all, mark the Health Centre. Perhaps make that 1. And then mark your position 2. Now, can you also help by assisting us by showing -- let me ask you this first: During this time, the summer of 1993, did you have occasion to be at or nearby Stela's headquarters, or the headquarters of this ATG that you say Stela was the commander of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: You want me to point at the house where the unit was stationed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, but we're doing this in two parts. First, answer my question. Were you, during this time, at or about this location where Stela's headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, I went past it every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us, please, on Exhibit P11.18 where that headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Up here on the corner here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mark that, please, with a number 3. And the last marking I'm going to ask you to make for now, unless the Chamber has questions, can you also mark where Baja's ATG, where his headquarters were, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It's here, on this corner here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you mark that, please, with a number 4. All right. Now, around this time -- that's all we're going to have at this moment about the ELMO. Thank you, Usher. Did you know under whose command -- and I'll ask you how -- but did you know under whose command the -- Stela's ATG was, I mean other than Stela? Who, above Stela, was in command of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It was Tuta, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, I'll come back to the how in just a moment, but do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know who was over Baja's ATG? Who was next up in the chain of command above Baja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Tuta again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell the Chamber, what do you base your answers on, that they were both under Tuta's control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, there are two reasons how which I know that. First, a day before the attack, Baja himself said that Tuta had issued the order. And secondly, because my brother was a member of the Benko Penavic ATG.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was -- just so we're clear, that was Baja's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, in the course of the summer of 1993, hear Stela say anything about who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any other HVO officers give orders to Stela in Mostar during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No, I'm sure about this, because once there was a meeting in my unit. We could ask why did we have to subordinate ourselves to what secret Stela's men were doing, and they told us we had no right to ask such questions, because he -- they could not decide what they would do, Baja and Stela, and that it all came from Tuta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever witness Stela resist taking orders from another HVO officer during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I really cannot recall that. I do not want to say -- to talk about something that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go forward. Do you know anything about a conversation between Stela -- and I'll, again, be very clear -- and this other Vinko Martinovic, Vina, during June or July 1993? And if there was such a conversation, will you tell the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I remember an action in which Baja's and Stela's men were to cross to the other side. I cannot tell you exactly when or where, but my friend and I were told that it would be good if we came out on top of one of those high, tall buildings near the Bulevar and to man the mortars, and that we did that because we had nothing to object to it. But Vina, after Stela left, Vina warned us that we had to mind our steps and take care of what we were doing because the war would be over one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, I'm only going to ask you about this once, and if you don't recall, I'll move further on. Do you remember any conversation between Stela and Vina about the use of mortars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it please the Court, this is a very leading and suggestive question, there's no question about it, and I strongly object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour --
